name: Question 5
worked_solution:
First, let's recall the sum and difference formulas for cosine:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha -\beta ) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡\beta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡\beta  \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha +\beta ) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡\beta -\operatorname{sin}⁡\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡\beta \end{aligned}
$$

Adding these equations, we get the following product-to-sum identity:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha -\beta )+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha +\beta ) & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡\beta  \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡\beta  & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha -\beta )+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha +\beta ))\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(13x)\operatorname{cos}⁡(8x) & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(13x-8x)+\operatorname{cos}⁡(13x+8x)) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(5x)+\operatorname{cos}⁡(21x)).\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this into the integral gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \operatorname{cos}⁡(13x)\operatorname{cos}⁡(8x)\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(5x)+\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(21x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{10}\operatorname{sin}⁡(5x)+\frac{1}{42}\operatorname{sin}⁡(21x)+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is an arbitrary constant.

First, let's recall the sum and difference formulas for cosine: cos⁡(α−β)=cos⁡αcos⁡β+sin⁡αsin⁡βcos⁡(α+β)=cos⁡αcos⁡β−sin⁡αsin⁡β

Adding these equations, we get the following product-to-sum identity: cos⁡(α−β)+cos⁡(α+β)=2cos⁡αcos⁡βcos⁡αcos⁡β=12(cos⁡(α−β)+cos⁡(α+β))

Thus, we have cos⁡(13x)cos⁡(8x)=12(cos⁡(13x−8x)+cos⁡(13x+8x))=12(cos⁡(5x)+cos⁡(21x)).

Substituting this into the integral gives ∫cos⁡(13x)cos⁡(8x)dx=∫12cos⁡(5x)+12cos⁡(21x)dx=110sin⁡(5x)+142sin⁡(21x)+C, where C is an arbitrary constant.
